content: 1. Continued breastfeeding during the second year of life, compared to stopping breastfeeding after 12 months, has been studied for its effects on child development, growth, morbidity, mortality, and maternal health. 2. The authors of this review include Tarun Gera, Dheeraj Shah, Rajesh K. Meena, and Harshpal S. Sachdev, all of whom are experts in pediatrics and clinical epidemiology based in New Delhi, India. 3. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life is well-documented to have significant benefits for child survival and health. 4. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of continued breastfeeding into the second year of life compared to stopping breastfeeding after one year, focusing on health-related outcomes for both children and their mothers. 5. The databases searched for this review in December 2020 included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, African Index Medicus, CINAHL, and others. 6. The review included prospective and retrospective cohort studies with concurrent control groups, population-representative cross-sectional cohorts, nested case-control studies, and controlled before-after studies. 7. Randomized controlled trials and non-randomized trials with concurrent comparison groups were intended for inclusion, but no such studies met the inclusion criteria. 8. Studies without control groups, systematic or narrative reviews, and other types of case-control studies were excluded. 9. Eligible studies included children aged 12-23 months who were breastfed for at least nine months or had a mean/median breastfeeding duration of nine months, along with their mothers. 10. The intervention was defined as continued breastfeeding beyond 12 months, with a minimum mean/median duration of 15 months, compared to no breastfeeding after 12 months. 11. Two review authors independently assessed study eligibility, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias using the Risk of Bias for Nutrition Observational Studies (RoB-NObs) tool. 12. Child outcomes assessed included development, growth, body composition, infections, non-infectious morbidity, nutritional status, bone health, oral health, and allergies/asthma. Maternal outcomes included cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular health, bone health, and mental health. 13. A total of 170 records from 146 studies were included, while 412 full-text records were excluded after screening 19,211 de-duplicated records. 14. Of the 146 included studies, 93 provided data on child outcomes, and 54 provided information on maternal outcomes. 15. Most studies had moderate to severe risk of bias due to confounding, participant selection, exposure classification, deviations from intended exposure, and missing data. However, the majority had low risk of bias in outcome measurement and selection of reported results. 16. Evidence on the effects of continued breastfeeding beyond 12 months on child and maternal health outcomes was of very low certainty, indicating significant uncertainty about its benefits or harms. 17. Continued breastfeeding into the second year of life may not provide substantial advantages or disadvantages for child or maternal health compared to stopping breastfeeding before one year. 18. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), continued breastfeeding into the second year may be associated with lower odds of overweight/obesity without increasing the risk of undernutrition. 19. Prolonged breastfeeding has been linked to childhood dental caries, emphasizing the need for proper oral hygiene in children breastfed beyond one year. 20. Due to the very low certainty of evidence, further research through well-controlled interventional studies is necessary to clarify these outcomes. 21. Breastfeeding for the first six months of life has well-established benefits for child health, but the advantages of continued breastfeeding into the second year remain uncertain. 22. Evidence is inconsistent regarding the benefits of prolonged breastfeeding for maternal health, such as reducing the risk of cardiovascular diseases and cancer. 23. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends breastfeeding for at least two years, but many mothers stop breastfeeding after the first year. 24. Breastfeeding beyond the first year has been associated with reduced risks of diarrhea, respiratory infections, and related mortality due to the bioactive compounds in human milk that enhance immunity. 25. Continued breastfeeding may also support cognitive development in children due to the presence of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs) essential for myelination and neuronal growth. 26. Breastfeeding has been linked to reduced risks of breast and ovarian cancer in mothers, improved postpartum weight loss, and better metabolic health. 27. Breastfeeding is associated with improved maternal mood, reduced stress, better sleep quality, and lower incidence of postpartum depression, potentially due to the anxiolytic effects of oxytocin. 28. Despite the documented benefits of sustained breastfeeding, it is not universally accepted as a health practice, partly due to inconsistent evidence and concerns about potential harms, such as malnutrition in LMICs. 29. The formulation of universally acceptable guidelines on breastfeeding duration requires updated, systematically reviewed evidence with GRADE classification on the benefits and harms of sustained breastfeeding for mothers and children. 30. Continued breastfeeding into the second year of life should be considered based on the feasibility and preferences of mothers and families, given the current uncertainty in evidence.
